公共设施巡检试点工作通知

为提升公共设施运行保障水平，现就开展巡检试点工作通知如下。本次试点在4个片区同步实施，周期为12周，覆盖
道路照明、护栏、井盖与休憩设施等类别。各参与单位应统一台账口径，明确责任分工，按本通知要求报送巡检记
录与问题处置情况，确保试点数据可比、过程可追溯。
1 试点目标与总体安排

试点以形成可复制的巡检机制为目标，重点验证巡查频次、问题上报与闭环处置的衔接效果。总体安排分为部署、
运行、评估三个阶段，各阶段任务由牵头单位统筹推进。参与单位应在本通知印发后按要求启动准备，运行期间保
持记录连续，评估阶段提交完整台账，避免中途更换统计口径。
1.1 巡检范围与对象分类

巡检范围以试点片区内的公共设施为限，按结构安全、功能完好、外观整洁三类要素划分对象。牵头单位应结合设
施分布确定重点点位，对高风险部位提高查看密度。分类结果作为排班与记录的依据，任何调整须经片区负责人确
认后生效，并在台账中注明调整原因与时间。
1.1.1 巡检组织与职责分工

试点实行片区负责制，每个片区设巡检小组，由组长、巡查员与记录员构成。组长负责排班与复核，巡查员负责现
场查看与初步判定，记录员负责当日录入与凭证归档。牵头单位负责统一标准与抽查，参与单位负责人员到位与设
备保障，职责边界应在启动前书面明确。
1.1.1.1 现场巡检执行要求

现场巡检应按照既定路线逐点查看，重点核对设施完好状态与周边环境风险。发现异常应立即拍照留证并填写问题
描述，能够现场处置的当场处理，不能处置的按程序上报。巡查员不得代填他人记录，记录员应在当日完成录入，
确保现场情况与台账信息一致、可复核。
1.1.1.1.1 巡查路线与频次安排

巡查路线按片区地理顺序编排，兼顾重点点位与盲区覆盖，避免重复往返。频次依据设施类别与风险等级确定，高
风险对象加密查看，一般对象按常规节奏执行。路线与频次一经确定应保持稳定，确需调整的由组长提出，经片区
负责人同意后更新排班表并通知全体巡查员。
1.1.1.1.2 问题发现与现场处置

问题发现后应先判定风险等级，涉及通行安全的立即设置临时警示并通知相关维护力量。轻微缺陷可纳入常规维修
计划，重大隐患须在2日内完成上报与初步处置。现场处置情况应如实记录处置人、处置方式与结果，未闭环事项须
注明责任单位与预计完成时间。
1.1.1.2 记录填报与信息归档

巡检记录采用统一表单，包含点位编号、查看时间、设施状态、问题描述与处置结果等字段。记录员应逐项填写，
不得空缺关键字段，照片与表单按点位对应归档。归档资料由片区保存备查，牵头单位按需要调阅，凡涉及后续评
估的数据应保持原始形态，不得事后修改。
1.1.2 抽查复核与质量把关

牵头单位组织抽查复核，重点核对记录完整性与现场实际情况是否一致。抽查采取随机选点方式，覆盖各片区与各
类设施，发现问题应反馈至片区并限期说明。复核结果作为试点评估的重要依据，对记录失实或漏报情形应如实登
记，并在阶段小结中说明整改情况。

1.1.2.1 复核时限与反馈流程

抽查复核的时限要求应明确到日。片区收到复核反馈后，须在2个工作日内就差异情况作出说明；牵头单位在收到说
明后5个工作日内完成复核确认，并将结论反馈片区。整个流程应留痕可查，确保每次复核都有明确的责任人与完成
时间，避免问题积压影响试点评估进度。
1.1.2.2 复核抽样覆盖与样本量

为保证复核结果具有代表性，抽查应覆盖全部4个试点片区，累计抽取样本不少于240个，兼顾各类设施与不同巡检
时段。抽样时优先选取记录存在疑点或问题上报较集中的点位，同时保留一定比例的常规随机样本，使复核既能发
现薄弱环节，又能反映整体记录质量水平。
1.2 阶段小结与信息报送

各片区应按阶段提交小结，说明巡检开展情况、发现问题的类别分布与处置进展。报送内容以台账数据为准，避免
主观概括替代事实记录。牵头单位汇总后形成试点简报，供参与单位对照改进。报送时间与格式由牵头单位统一通
知，逾期未报的应说明原因并补报。
2 试点评估与数据核验

评估围绕巡检覆盖、问题闭环与记录质量三个方面展开，以台账和抽查结果为证据来源。评估应区分观测到的记录
情况与对效果的推断，避免将相关性表述为因果结论。核验中发现的口径差异应逐项说明，评估结论须注明适用范
围与局限，供后续推广决策参考。

相关记录与要求见表 2。
2.1 评估指标与观测口径

评估指标包括点位覆盖情况、问题上报数量与闭环比例、记录完整程度等，均以试点期间台账为统计基础。各指标
应明确统计区间与计数规则，同一问题多次上报的按首次登记计。指标数值仅反映试点范围内的观测结果，不宜直
接外推至其他片区或更长周期。

2.1.1 样本抽取与核验方法

核验采用抽样方式，从各片区台账中抽取点位进行现场比对，样本总量为240个点位，覆盖各类设施与不同时段。核
验人员独立记录比对结果，与原始台账逐项对照。对不一致情形应记录差异类型，不预设原因结论，待汇总后统一

2.1.1.1 核验结果记录与比对

核验结果按点位逐条记录，包含台账信息、现场情况与差异说明。比对以事实描述为主，对无法现场确认的事项标
注待核，不强行归类。汇总时按差异类型统计出现次数，作为记录质量的观测依据。核验人员应在记录上签署姓名
与日期，确保过程可追溯。

2.1.1.1.1 差异说明与整改跟踪

对核验中发现的差异，片区应逐项说明形成原因，区分记录疏漏、信息传递偏差与现场变化等情形。整改措施应明
确责任人与完成时限，完成后由记录员更新台账并留存凭证。跟踪情况纳入下一阶段小结，未按期完成的应说明进
展，不得以口头说明替代书面记录。

2.1.1.1.2 数据局限与解释边界

试点数据来源于有限片区与有限周期，样本代表性存在局限，观测到的差异可能受时段、天气与人员安排等因素影
响。评估报告应明确说明这些限制，将描述性统计与原因推断分开表述，不得据试点结果直接断言推广后的效果，
相关判断需以后续更大范围验证为依据。
2.1.1.2 评估结论形成与复核

评估结论由牵头单位汇总核验记录后形成，初稿应提交各片区核对事实性内容。复核重点在于数据引用是否准确、
表述是否超出证据范围。对存在争议的条目应保留不同意见并注明依据，结论定稿后随试点简报一并印发，作为机

2.1.2 成果应用与机制完善

试点成果主要用于完善巡检标准、优化排班方式与改进记录表单。牵头单位应结合评估结论提出具体修订建议，明
确采纳与否的理由。涉及跨片区协同的事项，应在总结中提出衔接安排。成果应用不替代现行管理制度，相关调整
按程序报批后实施。
2.2 后续推广与工作衔接

试点结束后，牵头单位应提出后续推广的初步意见，说明适用条件与需补充的准备事项。推广前宜先小范围验证修
订后的标准与表单，再逐步扩大范围。各参与单位应做好人员交接与资料移交，确保台账连续完整，为后续工作提
供可靠基础。

仓储机器人的充电与任务分配

本文围绕仓储机器人在连续作业中的电量约束与任务分配展开，重点讨论充电决策如何影响拣选效率
与车队均衡。研究以240个模拟任务片段与4个模拟作业区为对象，区分可观测的调度记录与因果推断
的边界。全文先说明问题背景与观测口径，再给出充电阈值与任务派发的联合规则，最后报告模拟结
果并列出尚待验证的问题。
相关记录与要求见表 2。
相关记录与要求见图 1。
A 问题背景与观测口径
图 1：后续验证的分组安排与观察指标

仓储机器人电量耗尽会导致任务中断与通道拥堵，因此充电时机与任务派发必须协同考虑。本文采用
模拟观测口径，记录每台机器人的电量区间、等待时长与任务完成情况，但不把相关性直接解释为因
果效应。为避免口径漂移，所有记录均按统一时间窗对齐，并保留原始日志以便复核。
相关记录与要求见图 2。
图 2：研究范围与观测口径的界定条目
A.1 充电阈值与排队规则

充电决策采用分级阈值：电量低于警戒值时进入充电队列，高于恢复值时返回任务池。排队规则按剩
余任务紧迫度与充电桩占用情况排序，避免多台机器人同时涌向同一充电位。该规则为可调参数，本
文仅说明其设定逻辑，不宣称其优于其他策略。

A.2 任务派发的匹配方法

任务派发采用就近匹配与电量约束联合筛选：先按距离生成候选集合，再剔除电量不足以完成往返的
机器人。匹配结果记录候选数量与被剔除原因，用于后续分析。该方法属于启发式规则，本文不将其
表述为最优解，只作为可复现的模拟基线。

图 3：任务派发候选筛选的判定条件
B 模拟结果与讨论

模拟结果显示，充电等待与任务积压存在同步波动，但这一同步并不能直接证明充电规则导致了积压
变化。讨论部分区分两类结论：一类是可从日志直接核对的观测事实，另一类是需对照实验才能支持
的因果主张。本文仅报告前者，并把后者列为后续验证方向。
相关记录与要求见表 3。
B.1 指标对照与记录检查

指标对照表用于检查各作业区的记录完整性与口径一致性，包括充电次数、平均等待与任务完成比例
等条目。表中数值均来自模拟记录，用于内部核对，不作为对外绩效结论。若某作业区记录缺失，应
在复核后补齐再纳入对照。

B.2 局限与后续验证

本文的局限在于模拟环境简化了通道拥堵与人工干预，样本覆盖也有限。后续工作拟引入对照分组，
分别调整充电阈值与派发规则，以分离各自影响。在完成对照之前，任何关于效率提升的表述都应保
持谨慎，并明确标注为待验证假设。

寒驰冷链物流有限公司年度经营报告

本报告总结寒驰冷链物流有限公司在2025年度的整体经营表现，涵盖业务拓展、运营效率、财务成果与未
来规划。报告基于公司内部管理数据与经模拟审计的财务记录编制，旨在向股东、合作伙伴及管理层提供
透明、系统的年度回顾。报告期内，公司实现营业收入121.57百万元，营业成本79.02百万元，经营结余4
2.55百万元，较上年稳步提升，反映出冷链市场需求持续增长与公司服务能力的增强。
相关记录与要求见图 1。
A 业务回顾与运营分析

公司业务覆盖食品、医药及生鲜电商三大冷链板块，通过区域仓储网络与干线运输资源整合，为客户提供
一体化温控物流解决方案。运营团队持续优化路由规划与库存周转，提升车辆装载率与冷库利用率。年内
新增多个长期服务协议，客户结构进一步多元化，为收入增长奠定基础。
A.1 仓储与运输网络优化

公司对现有冷库布局进行重新评估，在核心消费区域增设前置仓，缩短末端配送半径。运输环节引入动态
温控监测系统，实现全程温度可追溯，降低货损率。通过整合往返线路与提升回程装载率，单位运输成本
得到有效控制，客户满意度同步提升。

A.2 客户服务与质量管控

公司建立客户服务快速响应机制，设定2个工作日内解决常规投诉的目标，并定期开展客户满意度调研。
质量管控方面，严格执行冷链温度记录与异常报警流程，全年未发生重大温控事故。针对医药冷链客户，
额外实施专项验证与定期审计，确保合规运营。
B 财务表现与经营成果

报告期内，公司营业收入达到121.57百万元，较2022年的78.16百万元实现显著增长，年均复合增长率保
持稳健。营业成本随业务规模扩大而上升至79.02百万元，但成本增速低于收入增速，推动经营结余提升
至42.55百万元。公司现金流状况良好，为后续资本开支提供保障。

B.1 收入与成本结构分析

收入构成中，食品冷链服务占比最高，医药冷链与生鲜电商增速较快。成本方面，运输费用与仓储租金为
主要支出项，人力成本随业务扩张同步增加。公司通过集中采购与节能改造，部分抵消了成本上涨压力，
毛利率维持在合理区间。

B.2 风险因素与应对策略

公司面临的主要风险包括燃油价格波动、冷链设施投资回收周期较长以及行业竞争加剧。为此，公司采取
签订长期运输协议锁定部分成本、分期投入自动化设备、拓展高附加值医药冷链客户等措施，以增强抗风

服务运营情境考核试卷

本试卷用于评估考生在服务运营情境中综合运用调度、质量、容量与补救知识的能力。考试时长与课程安排一
致，教学周为12周，共24次课、48学时。试卷包含情境选择题、计算分析题与案例决策题，所有数据均为模拟
情境，不涉及真实机构。考生须在答题纸上写明推理步骤，仅给出结论不得分。
相关记录与要求见表 3。
1 试卷说明与答题规范

本卷共分两部分：情境判断与计算分析。考生须使用黑色签字笔作答，计算题保留两位小数。试卷中出现的产
出、成本与结余数据均为模拟指标，仅用于考核分析能力。答题时须先列出关键假设，再给出计算过程，最后写

Discrete Event Simulation Course Syllabus

This syllabus defines a 12-week course in discrete event simulation delivered across 24
sessions and 48 teaching hours. It sets out learning outcomes, the weekly schedule,
laboratory expectations, assessment weightings and academic conduct rules. Students
learn to model queueing and service systems, build event calendars, validate models
against observations and report findings with appropriate uncertainty language. All figures
in this document are simulated planning values for instructional design purposes.

1 Course Design and Learning Outcomes

The course is organized around a build-measure-explain cycle. Each week pairs a short
conceptual lecture with a hands-on laboratory, so students encounter theory and
implementation together. By the end, learners should be able to translate a process
description into an event-driven model, justify input distributions, and distinguish simulated
outputs from causal claims about real systems. Instructors review drafts within 5 working
days to keep feedback timely.
Supporting records are presented in Table 2.
1.1 Weekly Topic Sequence

Topics progress from foundational mechanics to interpretation. Early weeks cover event
scheduling, random number generation and entity flow; middle weeks address input
modeling, warm-up periods and replication; later weeks focus on validation, sensitivity
analysis and communicating results. The sequence assumes no prior simulation software
experience but expects comfort with basic probability and programming constructs such as
loops and records.
Supporting records are presented in Table 1.
1.1.1 Event Scheduling and Queue Mechanics

This unit examines the event calendar as the engine of any discrete event model. Students
implement a priority queue of events, trace entity arrivals and departures, and observe how
service discipline changes waiting behavior. Laboratory exercises require a trace log
showing each event time and state change, so that instructors can verify understanding of
simultaneity and tie-breaking rules rather than only final averages.
1.1.2 Random Variates and Input Modeling

Students generate variates from uniform, exponential and empirical distributions, then fit
candidate distributions to provided arrival and service records. The unit stresses

convenience. Exercises ask learners to compare fitted models against held-out observations
and to explain, in plain language, why a good fit does not by itself prove the underlying
process behaves that way.

Validation activities compare model behavior with recorded system observations and
structured expert review. Students perform face validation, trace-driven checks and simple
sensitivity sweeps on key parameters. The unit emphasizes reporting ranges and caveats
alongside point estimates, and it explicitly separates what the simulation observed from
what may be inferred about the real system. Deliverables include a validation log with
decisions and rejected alternatives.

1.2.1 Trace-Driven Validation Exercises

Students replay recorded system traces through their models and compare simulated
outputs against observed values. Exercises use a sample of 240 observations drawn from 4
sites across 2022 to 2025, giving a realistic basis for discrepancy analysis. Teams document
each mismatch, classify its likely source, and decide whether to adjust logic, parameters, or

accept the deviation with a stated caveat in the validation log.
1.2.2 Sensitivity Sweeps and Reporting Ranges

Sensitivity sessions vary key inputs across plausible bounds and record how outputs
respond, such as output values moving from 79.55 to 119.76 and costs from 51.71 to
77.84. Students summarize results as ranges with caveats rather than single point
estimates, and they practice separating what the simulation observed from what may be
inferred about the real system when presenting findings.
2 Assessment and Laboratory Schedule

Assessment combines laboratory submissions, a midterm modeling task and a final project
with a written report and short presentation. Weights and due dates appear in the schedule
table below. Late work is accepted within 2 days of the deadline with a documented
penalty, and regrade requests must be filed within 5 days of feedback release. The final
project replaces a traditional closed-book examination.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 3.
2.1 Assessment Components and Weightings

Each component targets a distinct skill: laboratories test implementation discipline, the
midterm tests modeling judgment under time pressure, and the final project tests
end-to-end reasoning from problem framing to reported conclusions. Rubrics are published
at the start of term. Students receive formative feedback on at least two laboratory
submissions before the midterm, ensuring they can adjust before higher-stakes work
begins.
2.1.1 Laboratory Submissions

Laboratories are submitted as reproducible scripts plus a short memo. The memo must
state model scope, input assumptions, replication count and observed output ranges, using
the reporting template distributed in week one. Graders check that scripts run without
manual edits and that memos avoid overclaiming. Partial credit is available for correct
mechanics with incomplete interpretation, reflecting the course emphasis on both building
and explaining.
2.1.2 Final Project and Presentation

The final project asks teams to model a chosen service process, validate it against supplied
or collected observations, and present findings with explicit limitations. Presentations are
brief and followed by questions on assumptions and alternative explanations. Teams must
show at least one sensitivity check and one rejected modeling choice, demonstrating that
conclusions were tested rather than asserted. A shared repository preserves scripts and
logs for review.

1 土壤水分监测控制器操作总则

本总则说明土壤水分监测控制器的适用范围与操作责任。控制器用于田间多点土壤含水率的采集、显
示与灌溉联动，操作人员须经培训后方可上电调试。所有操作以本手册为准，涉及参数变更须填写记
录并由值班负责人复核。设备部署于户外环境，操作前应确认供电、接地与防雷状态，任何异常均须
停机排查，禁止带故障运行。
1.1 设备组成与工作原理

控制器由传感探头、采集主板、显示面板与联动输出模块构成，通过介电常数变化推算土壤体积含水
率。采集周期由内部时钟统一调度，数据经滤波后写入本地存储并上传至管理平台。操作人员应理解
采集、换算与输出三段流程的关系，明确探头埋设深度与代表性，避免将单点读数直接当作整块田地
的水分结论。
1.1.1 面板与接口识别

前面板包含显示区、状态指示灯与操作按键，背板提供探头接口、联动输出端子与通信口。识别接口
时须对照丝印标识，探头线缆按编号对应通道，禁止混插。状态灯以颜色区分运行、采集与告警状
态，操作人员应在交接班时核对灯态与屏幕信息是否一致，发现灯态与读数矛盾时先记录再排查，不
得随意短接端子。
1.1.1.1 首次上电与自检流程

首次上电前应检查线缆紧固、探头埋设与供电电压，确认无误后合闸。控制器启动后自动执行自检，
依次检测采集通道、存储与输出回路，自检结果在屏幕逐项显示。操作人员须逐项确认通过状态，任
一项目未通过即停止后续配置并记录故障现象。自检通过后方可进入参数设置，首次配置建议在白天
进行以便观察联动输出动作。
1.1.1.1.1 通道配置与探头标定

通道配置决定每个探头接口对应的地块与深度，须与田间布点图一致。探头标定采用烘干法对照，取
代表性土样测定实际含水率并与读数比对，形成修正系数后写入通道参数。标定应覆盖不同质地与深
度，记录标定日期与操作人。未标定通道的数据仅作趋势参考，不得作为灌溉决策依据，标定周期建
议与作物生育期同步安排。
1.1.1.1.1.1 单点标定的操作步骤

单点标定先在目标深度取样，装入密封盒送检，同时读取控制器瞬时值并记录时间。待烘干结果返回
后计算偏差，若偏差超出允许范围则调整该通道修正系数并复测。操作中须保持取样点与探头位置一
致，避免扰动周边土壤。每次标定结果填入标定记录表，注明土样编号、深度与修正值，复测通过后
方可启用该通道数据。
1.1.1.1.1.2 多点标定与系数写入

多点标定在同一地块选取若干代表点，分别取样与读数，汇总后拟合修正关系。拟合前应剔除明显异
常点并说明理由，系数写入前须由第二人复核数值与通道对应关系。写入后逐通道回读确认，防止串
号。多点标定结果反映地块整体偏差，操作人员应保留原始记录以便追溯，系数变更后应观察数个采
集周期再判断效果。

1.1.1.2.2 存储余量监控与补传操作

控制器本地存储写满后将覆盖最早记录，造成历史数据缺失。操作人员应每周查看存储余量，当剩余
空间低于三成时及时导出并清理。若上传中断，应先确认网络与时间同步状态，再启动补传，补传完
成后核对记录条数与时间戳连续性。跨设备比对前须确认各控制器时钟一致，避免因时间偏差导致同
一时段数据错位，影响后续分析与阈值复核。
1.1.2 报警与异常状态处理

控制器对探头断线、读数越界、存储异常与输出故障发出报警。操作人员接到报警后应先查看报警代
码与发生时间，再按代码对照排查，禁止直接清除报警而不记录。读数越界需结合近期降雨与灌溉判
断是否为真实变化，探头断线应检查接头与线缆。无法现场排除的故障应上报并做好标识，故障期间
的数据缺口须在记录中注明。
1.2 日常巡检与维护要点

日常巡检包括外观检查、灯态核对、读数合理性判断与线缆紧固检查。巡检应按规定路线逐点进行，
发现探头周围土壤开裂或积水须及时处理。清洁显示面板时使用干布，禁止用水冲洗机体。维护后须
复核对时钟与通道状态，并在巡检记录中签名。长期停用时应断开输出回路并做好防潮措施，重新启
用前按首次上电流程执行自检。

2.1.1.1 趋势判读与阈值复核

趋势判读关注含水率的持续下降或异常抬升，并结合阈值设置判断联动是否合理。若频繁启停或长期
不触发，应复核回差与延时参数，而非直接调整阈值。复核须在完整灌溉周期后进行，比较调整前后
数据分段。判读结论应注明样本时段与点位代表性，对单点异常先排查探头再讨论阈值，避免以个别

2.1.1.1.1 观测记录与因果说明

应明确哪些是观测到的读数变化，哪些是对原因的推测，两者不得混写。因果判断需有多源证据支

2.1.1.1.1.1 点位差异的对照方法

点位差异对照采用同期同深度比较，先统一时间窗口与修正系数版本，再比较各通道均值与波动幅
度。差异明显时应检查埋设深度、土壤质地与遮挡情况，排除安装因素后再讨论水分差异。对照结果
以表格呈现各点位特征，避免仅凭单次读数下结论。对照分析应保留原始序列，便于后续复核时重新
计算，不得只保留汇总值。

2.1.1.2 报表复核与归档要求

报表复核由非编制人执行，重点检查数据口径、缺失说明与结论边界。复核意见须书面记录，修订后

Fictional Equipment Maintenance Services
Agreement

This agreement records the simulated maintenance arrangement between the
service provider and the equipment owner for the covered production assets at
the named sites. It sets out the service scope, response duties, reporting
expectations and payment terms that govern the working relationship. The
parties acknowledge that all figures used in this document are simulated
indicators prepared for drafting review and do not describe real operating results.
1 Service Scope and Covered Assets

The provider shall maintain the covered equipment listed in the asset schedule,
including routine inspection, lubrication, calibration checks and replacement of
consumable parts. Coverage extends to the named production lines at each
registered site. Any asset added after signature requires a written scope
amendment signed by both parties before maintenance duties attach to it.
1.1 Preventive Maintenance Duties

The provider shall perform preventive maintenance visits on a published cycle,
following the manufacturer checklist for each asset class. Each visit includes
inspection, cleaning, adjustment and a written condition note. The owner shall
grant access during agreed windows and shall not operate covered assets with
known safety defects pending provider inspection.
1.1.1 Inspection Checklists and Records

Every preventive visit shall be documented on the standard checklist, recording
asset condition, parts replaced and any defects observed. Completed checklists
are delivered to the owner within the reporting window stated in the service
schedule. Records are retained for the agreement term and made available for
joint review on request.

This paper examines the design and
interpretation of urban heat sensing networks
that rely on a limited number of monitoring
sites. Sparse networks are common in practice
due to budget constraints, yet they raise
questions about representativeness and
inference. We draw on simulated deployments
to explore how site selection, sensor
placement, and statistical methods affect the
ability to characterize intra-urban temperature
variability. The analysis distinguishes between
observed patterns at monitored locations and
broader causal claims about urban heat,
emphasizing the need for cautious
extrapolation.

Background and Motivation

Urban heat islands pose significant risks to
public health and energy demand, but dense
monitoring is often infeasible. Many cities
operate only a handful of weather stations,
creating gaps in spatial coverage. This section
motivates the study by reviewing the
challenges of sparse sensing and the potential
for bias when using such data to inform policy.
We highlight the tension between cost and
coverage, and the need for methods that
make the most of limited observations.

Sparse Network Design
Considerations

Designing a sparse monitoring network
involves trade-offs between spatial coverage,
sensor accuracy, and cost. Key considerations
include the placement of sites to capture
representative microclimates, the use of
low-cost sensors versus reference-grade
instruments, and the frequency of data
collection. We discuss how network density
affects the ability to detect urban heat
patterns and the importance of metadata such
as land use and canopy cover at each site.

Site Selection and Sensor
Placement

Site selection is critical in sparse networks
because each location must serve as a proxy
for a larger area. We outline criteria for
choosing sites that maximize environmental
diversity, such as including parks, residential
areas, and industrial zones. Sensor placement
within a site also matters, as height and
exposure influence readings. The section
provides a checklist for evaluating site
representativeness and discusses common
pitfalls like locating sensors near heat sources.

Representativeness refers to how well a site
reflects the conditions of its surrounding area.
For sparse networks, this is a major concern

This guide sets how incoming service
tickets are classified, prioritised and passed
between shifts so that nothing is dropped at
handover. It applies to every queue in the
service desk and to all staff who triage, own
or receive tickets. The aim is consistent
decisions: the same ticket should reach the

is on duty. Where local practice differs, the
stricter rule applies until the guide is
formally revised.

A.1 Intake Channels and
Ticket Registration

Tickets arrive by portal form, email, phone
and walk-in. Each channel is registered in
the same system within the same working
day, and the registrar records the
requester, the affected service, the
observed symptom and any deadline
already promised. Email and phone reports
must be transcribed into the ticket body
rather than left in a mailbox. Duplicate

Warehouse Shift Handover and Inventory Guide

This guide sets out how shift supervisors at our distribution sites conduct handover and keep
inventory records consistent between crews. It covers the handover sequence, counting duties,
discrepancy escalation and the records that must survive each transition. Every procedure here
applies across the 4 operating sites and is reviewed on a 12-month cycle. Supervisors should
treat the written handover as the single authoritative record of what one shift passes to the next.
1 Handover Principles and Shift Boundaries

Handover is a controlled transfer of responsibility, not a conversation. The outgoing supervisor
remains accountable until the incoming supervisor signs the handover sheet, and the incoming
supervisor assumes custody of keys, seals and open tasks at that moment. Boundaries are fixed
by roster, and no shift may close without a countersigned sheet. Where a boundary is disputed,
the site manager decides and records the decision.
Supporting records are presented in Table 1.
1.1 Preparing Before the Boundary
Table 1: Shift boundary responsibilities by role

Preparation begins well before the boundary. The outgoing supervisor confirms that pick queues
are cleared or explicitly carried forward, that damaged goods are segregated, and that the dock
area is secured. Preparation checklists are completed in sequence so that nothing is signed off
prematurely. Any task that cannot be finished is written as a carry-forward item with a named
owner and a realistic completion window.
1.1.1 The Handover Walk and Verbal Briefing

The walk follows a fixed route through receiving, storage, packing and dispatch so that both
supervisors see the same conditions. The briefing then covers open orders, safety observations,
equipment faults and staffing gaps. Neither the walk nor the briefing replaces the written sheet.
Supervisors should keep the walk brisk but complete, pausing only where a physical condition
needs to be shown rather than described.

1.1.1.1 Confirming Physical and System Status

Physical status and system status are confirmed separately, then reconciled. The outgoing
supervisor demonstrates that seals are intact, that quarantine cages are locked and that scanner
devices are docked and charging. The incoming supervisor checks the warehouse management
system for open tasks and confirms that the system view matches what was seen on the walk.
Differences are noted before either supervisor signs.
1.1.1.1.1 Seals, Keys and Equipment Custody

Custody of seals, keys and powered equipment transfers only against a signature. Each item is
listed with its identifier and condition, and any missing item is escalated immediately rather than
noted for later. Equipment with a reported fault is tagged out and removed from the available
pool. The incoming supervisor confirms that chargers, batteries and access cards are accounted
for before releasing the outgoing crew.
1.1.1.1.2 Open Orders and Carry-Forward Tasks

Open orders are listed with order reference, priority and the reason they remain open.
Carry-forward tasks are limited to those that genuinely cannot be completed within the outgoing
shift, and each carries an owner and a deadline. The incoming supervisor may re-prioritise but
must record the change. Tasks carried forward repeatedly across shifts should be raised to the
site manager as a capacity signal.
1.1.1.2 Handover Sheet Completion and Signatures

The handover sheet is completed in full before either supervisor leaves the floor. It records the
boundary time, the walk findings, open orders, equipment condition and any escalations raised.
Both supervisors sign and time-stamp the sheet, and the incoming supervisor files it in the shift
log. Incomplete sheets are not accepted; a supervisor who cannot complete the sheet must
escalate to the site manager before departing.

1.1.2 Escalation During Handover

Some conditions cannot wait for the next routine review. Safety hazards, suspected theft, failed
seals and system outages are escalated to the site manager during handover, not after it. The
escalation is recorded with the time raised and the response received. Where the site manager is
unreachable, the duty manager acts, and the attempt and outcome are both written on the
sheet.
1.2 Handover Records and Retention

Completed handover sheets are retained in the shift log for audit and dispute resolution. Records
are stored so that any past shift can be reconstructed from the sheet, the system log and the
equipment register. Retention periods are set by site policy and reviewed with the cycle.
Supervisors should treat the log as evidence, writing entries that a reader unfamiliar with the
shift could follow without asking questions.
2 Inventory Counting and Reconciliation

Inventory accuracy depends on disciplined counting and honest reconciliation. Counts are
scheduled by zone and product class, and each count is performed by someone other than the
person who last handled the stock where staffing allows. Results are compared with system
balances, and every variance is investigated before an adjustment is posted. The guide treats
counting as a control activity, not a clerical chore.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 2.
Figure 2: Count method by zone type
2.1 Count Scheduling and Method

Counts are scheduled so that high-velocity zones are checked more often than slow-moving
storage. Counters use the approved method for each zone, whether full count, spot check or
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE

cycle count, and record the method used. Blind counts are preferred so that counters are not
anchored by expected figures. The schedule is published in advance and adjusted only with the
site manager's agreement.
2.1.1 Recording Count Results

Count results are recorded at the point of counting, not reconstructed afterwards. Each entry
shows the location, product reference, quantity observed and the counter's identifier. Corrections
are made by annotation rather than overwriting, so the original observation remains visible. The
incoming supervisor reviews recorded results during handover and flags any zone where
counting was interrupted or left incomplete.
2.1.1.1 Variance Investigation and Adjustment

A variance is investigated before any adjustment is posted. The investigator checks recent
movements, misplacements, unrecorded returns and possible scanning errors, and documents
which explanations were tested. Adjustments require approval from a supervisor who did not
perform the count. Where the cause cannot be established, the variance is recorded as
unexplained and monitored across subsequent counts rather than written off silently.
2.1.1.1.1 Locating Misplaced Stock

Misplaced stock is the most common explanation for a variance and should be sought before any
adjustment. The investigator searches adjacent locations, overflow areas and the quarantine
cage, and checks whether a put-away was scanned to the wrong bin. Findings are recorded with
the location where stock was actually found. Repeated misplacements in one zone point to
labelling or layout problems rather than individual error.
2.1.1.1.2 Approval and Posting of Adjustments

Adjustment approval is separated from counting and from stock handling. The approver reviews
the investigation record, confirms that plausible explanations were tested, and either approves,
queries or rejects the adjustment. Approved adjustments are posted promptly so that system
balances reflect reality before the next shift. Rejected adjustments return to the investigator with
a written reason, and the stock remains flagged until resolved.

2.1.1.2 Cycle Count Sampling and Coverage

Cycle counting samples a rotating portion of locations so that every zone is covered within the
review cycle. Sampling is planned rather than opportunistic, and coverage is tracked so that
neglected zones become visible. A sample of 240 location checks per cycle is the planning

reference for coverage across the 4 sites. Counters should not select their own samples, and
coverage gaps are reported at handover.
2.1.2 Discrepancy Escalation and Fraud Indicators

Most discrepancies are errors, but some patterns warrant escalation. Repeated shortfalls in one
product class, missing seals, or stock found outside recorded locations without explanation are
referred to the site manager. The guide does not treat these patterns as proof of wrongdoing;
they are indicators that require a documented review. Escalation records distinguish observed
facts from inferences drawn from them.
2.2 Improving Handover and Count Accuracy

Accuracy improves through small, sustained changes rather than periodic campaigns.
Supervisors should review handover sheets and count variances together to spot recurring
causes, such as unclear labelling or rushed boundaries. Suggestions are logged and reviewed at
the cycle review, and adopted changes are briefed at handover. Progress is judged by fewer
repeat variances and cleaner handover sheets, not by a single good week.

责任岗位的明确是整改闭环的前提。每项措施应指定执行人与验证人，二者分离有助于避免自评自证，也使验证

验证指标的选择应兼顾灵敏性与稳定性。过于敏感的指标易受短期扰动影响，过于稳定的指标则难以反映措施成

仓储协同运作能力综合考核试卷

本试卷用于检验考生在仓储协同场景中的综合判断与处置能力，考试时长以卷面说明为准，闭卷作
答。全卷围绕协同计划、库存共享、作业衔接与异常处置四个方向设题，考生须结合给定情境作答，
不得引用外部资料。评分关注决策依据是否清晰、责任划分是否明确、证据链是否完整，仅给出结论
而无推理过程的答案酌情扣分。
I 考核说明与作答要求

本部分说明试卷结构、作答规范与评分口径。全卷分为情境判断、方案设计与案例分析三组题型，考
生须在答题区域内书写，字迹清楚。涉及数量推算的题目应写明依据与步骤，涉及责任划分的题目应
指明承担主体与触发条件。凡答案与题设情境无关、或仅罗列术语而无具体处置措施的，按低档计
分。
情境判断题作答规范

情境判断题要求考生在给定条件下作出取舍并说明理由。作答时应先识别关键约束，再判断可选方案
的可行性，最后给出处置顺序。若情境中存在信息缺口，考生应明确指出需要补充的证据类型，而不
是凭假设直接下结论。评分时对理由与结论一致、约束识别准确的答案给予较高档次。
I.1.1 第一组情境判断题目

本组共设若干情境，均取自多仓协同的日常运作。考生需在有限时间内判断优先级并说明依据。题目
所给数据仅为情境设定，考生不得据此推断总体经营状况。作答时应区分可直接观测的现场事实与需
要进一步核查的推断，凡将推断表述为既定事实的，本组按规范性问题扣分。

This paper examines a practical
screening method for detecting incipient
mechanical faults in small industrial fans
using airborne acoustic signals. The
approach combines time‑domain
envelope statistics with spectral band
ratios to flag anomalies without
requiring contact sensors. We report
simulated observations from 240 fan
units across 4 sites, collected over 12
weeks. The study distinguishes
screening performance from causal
diagnosis, emphasizing that acoustic
flags indicate candidates for inspection
rather than confirmed root causes. All
numeric results are presented as
simulated indicators to illustrate the
workflow and decision thresholds.

1 Screening Framework and
Signal Processing

The screening framework processes
short acoustic recordings captured at a
fixed distance from each fan housing.
Signals are band‑pass filtered and
segmented into overlapping windows;
for each window we compute crest
factor, kurtosis, and the ratio of
high‑frequency to low‑frequency energy.
A two‑stage classifier first applies robust
z‑scores against a baseline built from
known‑good units, then a lightweight
decision tree refines borderline cases.
This design prioritizes low false‑negative
rates for screening while keeping
computational cost modest for edge
deployment.

1.1 Feature Extraction and
Baseline Construction

Baseline construction uses recordings
from fans confirmed healthy by
maintenance records. We extract
features in the time and frequency
domains, then normalize per unit to
reduce sensitivity to mounting and load
variations. The baseline is updated
incrementally as new healthy data
arrive, with a forgetting factor to
accommodate gradual drift. Feature
stability is assessed via intra‑class
correlation across repeated sessions;
features with low stability are

down‑weighted. This step is critical
because small fans exhibit broad
unit‑to‑unit variability even within the
same model.

Alert Logic

Alert thresholds are derived from the
distribution of baseline scores using a
percentile‑based rule, supplemented by
a persistence requirement to suppress
transient noise. An alert is raised only
when the score exceeds the threshold
for consecutive windows. We tuned the
persistence length and percentile using
simulated data to balance detection
latency against nuisance alerts. The

This notice sets out the binding arrangements for delivering the vocational skills
training programme during the 2025 cycle. It applies to all training sites, contracted
instructors and enrolled trainees, and replaces prior informal guidance. The
programme runs for 12 weeks with 24 sessions and 48 teaching hours, and must be

Site coordinators are accountable for compliance with every clause below.
1 Programme Scope and Training Objectives

The programme targets practical competency in the designated trade areas and is
limited to trainees who meet the entry criteria. Its objectives are to raise measurable
skill attainment, reduce workplace error rates and prepare trainees for assessment.
Training content must align with the approved curriculum and may not be
substituted without written approval. Each site must deliver the full 48 teaching
hours and document attendance against the session plan.

1.1 Delivery Schedule and Site Allocation

Delivery is organised across 4 training sites, each operating the same 12 week
schedule to preserve comparability. The schedule fixes 24 sessions per cohort, with
no more than two sessions in any single day. Site allocation follows trainee residence
and equipment availability; transfers require coordinator approval. Any deviation
from the published timetable must be recorded and reported within 2 working days
so that central monitoring remains accurate.

1.1.1 关键设施与系统边界

系统边界以水厂出水口为起点，经主干管、加压泵站至用户接入点为止。关键设施包括取水泵站、净水构

1.1.1.1 取水与净水环节

取水环节的韧性主要取决于水源数量与切换条件，净水环节则取决于工艺冗余与药剂储备。评估中发现，
部分水厂在单一水源受限时缺乏明确的切换时限要求，导致决策延迟。建议为每个水厂明确备用取水启用

取水口冗余配置应回答三个问题：备用取水口是否具备独立取水能力、切换所需时间是否可接受、切换后
水质是否仍满足净水工艺要求。评估记录显示，部分备用取水口长期未启用，设备状态与操作熟练度均存

1.1.1.1.2 净水工艺冗余与药剂储备

净水工艺冗余体现为构筑物可并联运行、关键设备可快速替换、药剂储备满足连续运行需要。评估建议按
最不利工况确定药剂最低库存线，并明确补货触发条件与责任人。储备量应以记录形式固化，避免因临时
调拨导致账面与实际不符，影响应急判断。
1.1.1.2 输配与加压环节

输配环节的韧性集中体现在管网连通度与加压泵站的备用能力。环状管网比例较高、阀门分区合理的区
域，故障隔离范围更小，恢复更快。评估建议对关键干管节点开展连通性复核，明确故障时的隔离顺序与

Demand Forecasting for Public Library Services

This paper examines how a four-site library
network can forecast demand for lending,
reference and programming services using
circulation logs, visitor counts and program
registrations. We treat forecasts as decision
aids rather than verdicts, and we separate
simulated observations from causal claims
throughout. The analysis covers data
preparation, model comparison, scenario
interpretation and the governance duties that
keep forecasts accountable to branch staff
and residents.

A Study Scope and
Forecasting Questions

The study addresses a practical question: how
many loans, visits and program seats should
each branch plan for in the coming cycle? We
frame forecasting as a planning instrument for
staffing, collection rotation and room booking,
not as a performance rating. The scope covers
the main circulating collections and public
programs across the participating sites, while
excluding interlibrary transfers and one-off
outreach events that follow their own
scheduling logic.
A.1 Data Sources and Preparation

Records come from circulation systems, door
counters and registration logs covering 2022
through 2025. We harmonize branch
identifiers, remove duplicate checkouts, and
flag closure days and system outages before
aggregation. Weekly series are constructed so
that holiday spikes are visible rather than
smoothed away, and every exclusion is logged
so that reviewers can reconstruct the
prepared dataset from the raw extracts.

A.1.2 Handling Closures and

Closure days, renovation periods and holiday
weeks create gaps that distort naive
averages. We mark these intervals explicitly
and model them as known absences rather
than missing demand. Where a gap exceeds a

A.2 Constructing Weekly Demand
Series

Weekly aggregates combine loans, visits and
program registrations into separate series
rather than a single composite index. Keeping
the series apart preserves interpretability: a
rise in visits without a matching rise in loans
suggests different service use. Each series
carries a data-quality flag, and weeks below a
completeness threshold are excluded from
model fitting but retained in the audit trail for
transparency.

B Model Comparison and
Validation

We compare a seasonal baseline, a regression
with calendar and weather covariates, and a
gradient-boosted model across the prepared
series. Validation uses rolling-origin splits so
that each model is tested only on weeks after
its training window. Accuracy is reported per
branch and per service line, because
aggregate scores can hide a branch where a
model consistently under-predicts weekend
demand.

B.1 Evaluation Metrics and Error
Patterns

Forecast error is summarized with mean
absolute percentage error and a bias measure
that reveals systematic over- or
under-prediction. Errors cluster around school
holiday transitions and program launch weeks,
which suggests calendar features deserve
more weight than weather variables. We also
report error by branch size, since small
branches show wider relative error even when
absolute differences are modest.

B.1.1 Backtesting Across Branches

Backtests replay 12 weeks of history for each
of the 4 sites, refitting models at fixed
intervals. Results show that the seasonal
baseline is competitive for loans but weaker
for program registrations, which respond to
announcement timing. These are simulated
backtest observations, not evidence that any
single model causes better service outcomes;
they indicate where model choice matters
most for planning.

B.1.2 Interpreting Forecast
Intervals

Point forecasts are presented with prediction
intervals so planners can see the plausible
range. A branch planning staffing against the
upper bound will over-staff on average, while
planning against the lower bound risks queues
at peak hours. We recommend choosing the
interval width according to the cost of being
wrong for each service, and we label intervals
as simulated estimates rather than
guarantees.

Forecasts enter branch planning only after a
review meeting where supervisors check
assumptions, note local events and record
dissent. The review produces a decision memo
with owners and review dates, and model

governance keeps forecasting accountable:
staff know which numbers drive rosters, and
residents can ask how service levels were set
without confronting an unexplained algorithm.

Recycling Service Pilot Implementation

This document sets out how the recycling service pilot will be implemented across
the participating collection sites, from mobilisation through review. It defines the
operating scope, the duties of the delivery team, the evidence that will be
gathered and the questions the review must answer. The pilot runs for 12 weeks
and is treated as a learning exercise: observations are recorded separately from
any causal claims about household behaviour or material recovery.
Pilot Purpose and Operating Scope

The pilot tests whether a revised collection and sorting arrangement can be
delivered reliably at the participating sites within the agreed service window.
Scope covers kerbside set-out, transfer to the sorting point, contamination checks
and resident communication. Activities outside this scope, including permanent
fleet procurement and long-term contract changes, are excluded and will be
considered only after the review reports its findings to the sponsoring committee.
Service Model and Collection Routes

The service model uses a fixed weekly route pattern with two collection passes
per site and a shared transfer point. Route sequencing was chosen to keep
vehicle dwell time short and to allow sorting staff to receive material in consistent
batches. Route supervisors record arrival and departure times at each stop so
that the review can compare planned and actual service delivery without
attributing differences to any single cause.
Site Readiness and Equipment

Each site must be confirmed ready before collections begin. Readiness covers bin
placement, signage, access for collection vehicles, staff briefing and a dry sorting
area. Site leads sign a readiness checklist and report exceptions to the pilot
coordinator, who decides whether a site starts on schedule or joins in a later
wave. Equipment shortfalls are logged and resolved before the first collection
pass.
Bin Allocation and Resident Communication

Bin allocation follows household size bands agreed with site leads, and every
household receives a short printed guide in plain language. Communication
covers set-out times, accepted materials and what happens when a bin is
rejected. Residents can raise questions through a local phone line, with responses
targeted within 2 working days. Messages are kept consistent across sites so that
the review can compare experiences fairly.

Contamination Checks at Set-Out

Collection crews carry out a visual contamination check at set-out and tag bins
that contain clearly non-accepted material. Tagged bins are recorded with a
reason code and left for the household to correct before the next pass. Crews do
not open sealed bags. The check is a service quality measure, not an
enforcement action, and households receive a follow-up note explaining the
correction needed.

Sorting Point Intake Records

The sorting point keeps an intake record for every batch, noting arrival time,
source site, estimated weight band and visible contamination. Records are
entered on the same day and cross-checked by a second staff member. Where a
batch is held back for inspection, the reason is written on the record. These
entries form the main evidence base for the review and are retained for the full
pilot period.

Route Contingency Arrangements

When a route cannot be completed, the supervisor activates a contingency plan
that prioritises households missed on the previous pass and defers non-urgent
transfers. Affected residents are notified the same day through the local phone
line and printed notice where needed. Each activation is recorded with the
trigger, the stops affected and the recovery date, allowing the review to assess
how often contingency arrangements were needed.
Site Readiness Evidence and Checks

Readiness evidence is collected through signed checklists, photographs of bin
placement and brief notes from site briefings. The coordinator samples completed
checklists to confirm that entries are consistent and that exceptions were
resolved. Evidence is filed by site and week, so that any later question about a
site's starting condition can be answered from the record rather than from
recollection.
Monitoring, Records and Reporting

Monitoring combines route logs, sorting point intake records and resident contact
notes. The pilot coordinator compiles a short weekly summary for the delivery
team and a fuller report at the end of the pilot. Records are kept in a single
shared register with clear ownership, and any gap is flagged at the next weekly
meeting so that it can be corrected while the relevant staff are still available.

Sampling and Observation Method

Observation uses a structured sampling approach across the participating sites,
with checks spread over the pilot period rather than concentrated in one week.
Observers follow a written checklist and record what they see without inferring
household intent. Simulated observations are labelled as such in the register, and
the review team is instructed not to treat observed associations as evidence of
cause and effect.
Data Handling and Quality Assurance

Data handling follows a simple rule: one entry, one owner, one date. The register
is reviewed weekly for missing fields, duplicate batch records and inconsistent
reason codes. A second reviewer checks a sample of entries against paper forms.
Corrections are made by annotation rather than deletion, so that the review can
see what changed and why, and the audit trail remains intact.

Record Gaps and Follow-Up Actions

When a record is missing, the coordinator raises a follow-up action with a named
owner and a due date. Actions are closed only when the missing entry is restored
or the gap is explained in writing. Recurring gaps are discussed at the weekly
meeting, since they often point to a form design problem or an unclear duty
rather than to individual error.
Interpreting Observed Patterns

Observed patterns, such as a rise in tagged bins during a particular week, are
reported as observations and not as proof that a communication change caused
the difference. The review team compares records across sites and weeks, notes
plausible alternative explanations and states clearly where the evidence is too
thin to support any conclusion about cause.
Review Questions for the Final Report

The final report must answer a fixed set of questions: whether the service ran as
designed, where records were incomplete, which adjustments were needed and
what residents asked about most often. It must also state what the pilot cannot
